strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: selecting among LLMs to trade off quality and cost, with clear motivation for moving beyond fixed centralized routers.

The proposed self-routing cascade is simple, intuitive, and practically appealing; the scenario-conditioned refusal mechanism is an elegant way to expose user preferences without retraining per scenario.

The empirical section is fairly broad, covering several in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, multiple cost-preference settings, and comparisons to relevant routing baselines such as FrugalGPT, AutoMix, FORC, RouteLLM, and GraphRouter.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond the main table, including reduced-agent experiments, routing distribution shifts, answered-vs-rejected accuracy, and a check that training does not substantially improve base task-solving ability.
Implementation details, prompts, dataset statistics, and baseline descriptions are mostly documented, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central novelty is somewhat overstated. In the actual experiments, DiSRouter is a sequential cascade with trained refusal behavior, not a general distributed routing network; tree/mesh routing and broader distributed-agent claims remain speculative.

The cost accounting is a major concern. The main utility metric ignores the cost of all rejection/routing calls in DiSRouter while counting additional verification overhead for AutoMix. Even if rejection time is small, excluding it from the primary metric can materially favor the proposed cascade, especially for queries that traverse several models.
The evaluation uses only one homogeneous model family, Qwen2.5-Instruct, so the claimed modularity, scalability, and generality to heterogeneous LLM pools are not well supported.

The “plug-and-play” claim is only weakly tested by removing agents. Adding or updating an agent would still require self-awareness training and calibration, which undermines the strongest flexibility claims.

The comparison between intrinsic self-assessment and external routers is not fully fair or conclusive: the intrinsic method benefits from modifying the target LLM with supervised/RL training, while the external classifiers are trained under a different formulation and resource budget.

The utility metric depends on manually assigned normalized costs and three selected alpha values; the paper would be stronger with real dollar/latency/token costs, Pareto-front analyses, and sensitivity to cost normalization and gamma.

The RL/SFT training process requires ground-truth correctness labels and repeated sampling from each target model, which may be expensive; this training cost and data-generation burden are not included in the practical efficiency discussion.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially that intrinsic self-awareness is inherently superior to external assessment and that the system is fully distributed, scalable, and robust. The experiments show a promising cascade, but not the broader paradigm.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: routing queries among LLMs to trade off accuracy and cost.
The proposed answer-or-reject cascade is simple, intuitive, and potentially practical when all candidate models can be fine-tuned.
The experiments cover several benchmark categories and compare against multiple routing baselines, with additional OOD and reduced-agent analyses.
The scenario-conditioning idea via cost-preference prompts is a reasonable mechanism for changing the routing aggressiveness without training separate systems.
weaknesses: The novelty is overstated. The evaluated system is essentially a fine-tuned abstention/cascade router, closely related to FrugalGPT-style cascades, AutoMix/self-verification, and prior refusal/self-awareness training. The broader claims about distributed routing networks are not actually evaluated beyond a linear cascade.

The cost accounting is a major concern. DiSRouter must run smaller models to generate rejections before reaching larger models, but the main utility ignores these cumulative routing costs and counts only the final model. The appendix argues rejection is short, but even small repeated costs can change the comparison, and the normalized cost values are not tied cleanly to actual latency or monetary cost.

The evaluation is potentially unfair and confounded: DiSRouter fine-tunes the candidate LLMs themselves using in-domain data, while baselines are mostly external routers. The paper lacks strong comparisons to calibrated abstention cascades, threshold-tuned self-routing baselines, or baselines given the same fine-tuning signal.

Several key claims are weakly supported. Modularity is tested only by removing models from a homogeneous Qwen cascade, not by adding new models, handling heterogeneous model families, or changing topology. The paper also excludes some baselines from the reduced-agent experiment because they would require retraining, which makes the modularity comparison incomplete.

The self-awareness analysis is not fully convincing. The answer/reject decision is trained directly for this behavior, so showing higher accuracy on answered than rejected examples is partly tautological. The external-router comparison uses a narrow binary setup for one 7B model and does not establish a general intrinsic-assessment advantage.

The theoretical formulation claims distributed optimization decomposes the global objective, but the local reward is heuristic and does not prove or guarantee optimal system-level routing under cascaded dependencies.

Results are aggregated across datasets with no variance, significance testing, or detailed per-dataset analysis in the main paper. Some gains are modest, and in OOD settings DiSRouter often pays substantially higher cost for limited utility improvements.

Reproducibility is incomplete: important details such as the sampling count N for SFT construction, exact splits, answer judging procedures, trained checkpoints, code availability, and full cost measurement protocol are missing or underspecified.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and timely idea: replacing a centralized LLM router with self-routing agents that decide whether to answer or defer. This is conceptually appealing for modular multi-model systems.
The method is simple and practical: rejection-based self-assessment plus scenario-conditioned prompts provides an intuitive mechanism for trading off accuracy and cost.
The experimental evaluation is fairly broad, covering multiple benchmarks, several router baselines, three cost/preference settings, out-of-domain datasets, and a reduced-agent modularity setting.

Results are consistently positive in utility, especially after RL, and the analysis of routing distributions, answered-vs-rejected accuracy, and external-vs-intrinsic assessment helps support the core claim that trained self-assessment is useful.

The paper is generally well organized and includes useful implementation details, prompts, dataset descriptions, baseline descriptions, and a check that task-solving ability itself does not substantially improve after training.
weaknesses: The central claim of distributed routing is only partially validated: the experiments instantiate a simple homogeneous Qwen cascade, not richer distributed topologies, heterogeneous providers, dynamically added models, or realistic multi-agent networks.

The cost model is a major simplification. Utility uses manually normalized fixed model costs and ignores the cumulative inference cost of rejected intermediate agents, even though DiSRouter requires smaller models to generate rejection responses before forwarding. The appendix argues this is small, but it is still part of the method's practical advantage claim.

The comparison to centralized routers is not fully apples-to-apples. DiSRouter fine-tunes every non-final candidate model with SFT and RL, while some baselines rely on a separate router; the training and deployment complexity of modifying all serving models is not incorporated into the claimed modularity/cost benefits.

The modularity experiment is limited to removing two agents from the same trained cascade. It does not demonstrate adding a new model, replacing a model with a different family, or preserving performance under genuine pool changes, which are key motivations of the paper.

The evaluation lacks variance estimates, statistical significance, and sensitivity analysis for important hyperparameters such as the rejection threshold, reliability factor gamma, cost normalization, and scenario prompt design.

The external-router comparison in Table 5 is suggestive but narrow: it focuses on one 7B model and a binary solvability setup, and may favor the proposed model because self-assessment is directly trained as the target behavior.

Claims such as superior scalability, robustness, and fully distributed optimization are stronger than what the experiments establish; the paper would be stronger if these were framed as promising properties rather than demonstrated conclusions.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: routing among heterogeneous LLMs to trade off accuracy and cost.
The proposed self-rejection/self-awareness training pipeline is simple, intuitive, and practically relevant for cascade-style model selection.

Experiments cover multiple QA/reasoning datasets, several user-preference settings, OOD datasets, a reduced agent pool, heterogeneous model families, and an appendix extension to open-ended summarization.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond headline utility, including answer/rejection accuracy, routing distributions, latency overhead, and a check that task capability is not substantially improved by the self-awareness training itself.
Results are consistently favorable in utility, especially by reducing cost while preserving reasonable accuracy, and the scenario-conditioned behavior is empirically demonstrated.
weaknesses: The main novelty is somewhat overstated. The implemented system is essentially a cascade with learned abstention/rejection behavior; the broader claims about distributed routing networks, tree/mesh topologies, and decentralized optimization are not experimentally validated.

The comparison to centralized routers is not fully satisfying because DiSRouter modifies and fine-tunes the candidate LLMs themselves, whereas many baselines use external routers over mostly fixed model outputs. This makes the comparison partly a training intervention versus router-only methods.

The cost model is simplified. Main utility tables ignore rejection/routing inference cost, and although appendix timing suggests this overhead is small, the utility conclusions depend on normalized fixed costs rather than actual end-to-end serving cost across tasks and deployment settings.

Baseline performance appears surprisingly weak for some methods, especially RouteLLM, and the paper does not provide enough evidence that all baselines were adapted and tuned to the same standard as the proposed method.

The theoretical formulation of distributed optimization is thin: the decomposition into independent local policies is asserted, but there is no proof that local reward optimization yields a globally optimal or stable routing policy.

Claims about plug-and-play modularity are only partially supported. Removing models is tested, but adding new models still appears to require self-awareness training, calibration, ordering, and scenario alignment.

The open-ended task extension is preliminary. It relies on BERTScore as a proxy reward, uses saturated model performances, and does not demonstrate end-to-end routing quality with human or stronger judge evaluation.

The paper would benefit from stronger ablations, such as SFT-only versus RL under matched answer rates, different gamma values, threshold sensitivity, training data size sensitivity, and direct comparison to per-model abstention classifiers trained with the same labels.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical problem: routing queries across LLMs to trade off accuracy and cost. The framing around model self-assessment and rejection is relevant and potentially useful.
The proposed SFT/RL pipeline is clearly described, with an intuitive reward design that conditions rejection behavior on a user preference parameter alpha.

The experiments include several router baselines, multiple datasets, in-domain and OOD evaluations, and some useful analyses of answer/reject behavior, latency overhead, reduced agent pools, and heterogeneous model families.
The empirical results show that the method can improve the reported utility metric over the compared baselines, especially after RL reduces cost while preserving much of the accuracy.
weaknesses: The central novelty is overstated. In the evaluated form, DiSRouter is essentially a trained abstention cascade where each model says either an answer or 'I don't know'; this is close to existing cascade, abstention, and self-verification routing ideas, while the broader 'distributed network' claim is not actually demonstrated beyond a simple ordered cascade.

The cost accounting is a serious concern. The main utility ignores intermediate rejection/inference costs in the cascade and uses fixed normalized costs, while the method requires running smaller models before larger ones for rejected queries. Appendix timing suggests overhead may be small in this setup, but the main comparisons are not based on true end-to-end compute, dollar cost, or latency and may favor the proposed method.

The comparison to centralized routers is not fully fair. DiSRouter fine-tunes the candidate LLMs themselves with 10k samples and RL, whereas several baselines are external routers trained under different assumptions. The paper does not compare against strong abstention/cascade baselines trained with the same data and objective, nor against calibrated confidence or selective prediction methods with comparable training budgets.

The evaluation uses Qwen2.5 models from the same family as the main setting, so the cascade benefits from monotonic size-performance assumptions. The heterogeneous and GPT experiments are relegated to appendices and are limited; the GPT-series result is actually weaker than some baselines in-domain and only modestly better OOD.

The claimed modularity and scalability are weakly supported. Removing agents without retraining is tested, but adding new agents, changing topology, non-monotonic model capabilities, domain-specialized models, and tree/mesh routing are mostly speculative.

The method requires per-model self-awareness training and RL, which is expensive and operationally burdensome. This undercuts the claim that the framework is more flexible than router retraining, since updating or adding a model may still require nontrivial alignment data and training.

The utility improvements are sometimes modest and driven by the chosen alpha/cost normalization. For example, OOD gains over GraphRouter/FrugalGPT in cost-first and balance settings are small, and accuracy often drops substantially relative to the largest model or SFT variant.

The paper's analysis of 'self-awareness' is not rigorous enough. Answer/reject classification against greedy correctness is an imperfect proxy, and using forced prefix injection to estimate rejected-query accuracy may change model behavior. Calibration, selective risk-coverage curves, and confidence/error tradeoffs would be more convincing.

The paper makes broad claims about intrinsic self-awareness, external router inferiority, and distributed optimization, but the formalism does not establish that independent local optimization yields globally optimal or robust routing behavior.

Reproducibility is incomplete: many implementation details are described, but exact train/test splits, sampled subsets, prompts for all tasks, reward parsing, evaluation scripts, and model checkpoints are not clearly provided in a way that would make the results easy to reproduce.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical problem: routing among LLMs with different accuracy-cost profiles, and the motivation for avoiding a fixed centralized router is clear and timely.

The proposed DiSRouter formulation is intuitive and useful: training each model to answer or abstain/reject creates a modular cascade that can adapt to different cost-performance preferences through prompting and reward design.

The empirical section is broad: the authors evaluate on multiple QA/reasoning benchmarks, compare against several routing baselines, include OOD results, reduced-agent experiments, overhead/latency analysis, self-awareness diagnostics, and extensions to heterogeneous model families and open-ended summarization.

The results are generally convincing in showing improved utility, especially after RL, and the analysis of answered-vs-rejected accuracy supports the core claim that the trained models learn a meaningful abstention behavior.
The paper is clearly written overall, with helpful figures and appendices that provide prompts, dataset statistics, baseline details, and additional ablations.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat overstated. In the actual experiments DiSRouter is primarily a learned abstention cascade, closely related to prior cascading, self-verification, and early-abstention routing methods. The broader claims about distributed networks, trees, and multi-agent topologies are mostly conceptual rather than demonstrated.

The main evaluation relies heavily on a single ordered Qwen2.5 model family and verifiable benchmark tasks. The heterogeneous and open-ended experiments are useful but remain relatively limited, so the generality of the method is not fully established.

The fairness of some baseline comparisons is hard to assess. Several baselines are modified substantially from their original implementations, and RouteLLM performs surprisingly poorly. More faithful or stronger implementations, plus clearer validation/model-selection protocols, would strengthen the evidence.

The utility metric depends on normalized model costs and ignores routing overhead in the main tables. Although the appendix argues the rejection overhead is small, the conclusions could change under API pricing, batched inference, throughput constraints, or settings where rejected-prefix generation is not negligible.

The modularity claim is only partially validated. Removing agents without retraining is shown, but adding new agents, updating a model, or routing among non-monotonic specialists is not evaluated in the main setting.

The self-awareness training requires labeled data and repeated sampling from each target model to determine answerability, which may be expensive and limits applicability to tasks where correctness can be automatically judged. This cost is not incorporated into the practical comparison.

Reproducibility is not fully demonstrated: the paper says components are public, but it is unclear whether code, trained checkpoints, exact data construction scripts, and all baseline configurations will be released.
